In the section on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the first part clarifies the inclusion of all phenomena (*dharmasaṃgraha*). The subsequent reasoning critiques errors as per the text.
"One should now... introduces the request for empowerment. The text has two parts: first, establishing the practice; second, requesting empowerment. Establishing the practice:
First, it is explained in general that the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) possess the power to destroy the perversions,
as in the text. Next, the four foundations of mindfulness are explained individually.
First, there are five kinds of impurity.
Regarding the initial listing of these five types of impurity,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 21, explains them in detail.
Regarding the first point, "seeds," as the verse of the treatise says:
"The seeds of this body are impure; they are not exquisite jewels."
It is not born from purity.
When the parents harbor perverse thoughts and recollections, the wind of desire fans the fire of lust;
the flesh, marrow, and fat flow and, through the heat of transformation, become semen.
Due to the causal conditions of karma, consciousness takes up residence within the seeds [of the embryo] amidst the red and white vital essences;
hence it is said that it "seizes the discarded body of another."
Regarding "emitting tears and so forth," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When the internal desire-worms of a man and woman unite, the white essence of the male worm emerges like tears."
The female worm is red and its essence is like vomit as it emerges;
the marrow-fat flows, causing these two worms to vomit tears as they emerge.
This refers to the impurity of the place of birth.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"This body is foul and impure; it does not arise from the blossoming of a flower, nor from the *campaka* tree, nor does it emerge from a mountain of jewels."
Regarding what is now called "place of abiding": that which is inhabited is termed "abiding" (sthāna),
and that which arises from it is termed "arising" (utpatti).
Therefore, these two passages convey but a single meaning.
"Vei" (猥) refers to that which is mixed with evil;
it also signifies multitude.
These are menial servants.
As for those who are mutually impure,
they [provide] clothing, bathing, various flowers, and incense.
Even delicacies such as sweetmeats and various exquisite flavors become impure within a single night; likewise,
even if one wears celestial garments and eats celestial food, they become so by the very nature of the body.
It would likewise become impure;
how much more so the clothing and food of humans?
As the verse in the treatise says:
The substances of earth, water, fire, and wind can transform and remove impurities;
yet even by emptying the oceans to wash this body, one cannot make it fragrant and clean.
It is like washing a dead dog with seawater.
Even if a single particle remains, it is as foul-smelling as before;
so too is the case with filth and excrement.
"Fen" (𦡲) refers to the stench of rotting matter.
Earwax; *miśra* is the congealed secretion of the eyes;
*liṇu* (urine) should be written as this [same] *miśra*.
It is precisely because of illness that its urine is foul-smelling; thus,
its intrinsic nature is impure.
The passages for excrement and urine, as well as the eyes, tears, mucus, and sleep, constantly flow without ceasing.
As a verse in the treatise says:
"Various kinds of impure things fill his body."
It constantly flows out without ceasing, like a leaking bag filled with things.
Regarding "pus" (nong):
the *Yupian* states:
An abscess is blood;
the flesh of the body is no different from it.
"Fat" refers to the smoothness and glossiness of the body.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states:
"That which has horns is called *zhi* (tallow); that which has no horns is called *gao* (lard).
The impurities within the body are categorized as being like these."
The Book of Rites says:
"Beef fat is rank;
chicken fat is fishy."
Mutton fat has a rank odor.
If one speaks of the stench of fish, one should say "xīng" (腐臭) or "yì" (腥).
"Fáng" (肪) refers to the fatty grease of a fat animal.
"Fat" (𦙽) is also adipose tissue.
What is now called "foul-smelling and acrid" (腥臊) refers to things such as dogs and chickens.
Therefore, the *Catuṛsmṛtyupasthāna* says:
The twelve external objects are called impure in terms of their characteristics;
the twelve internal objects are called impure in terms of their nature;
the twelve intermediate objects are called impure in terms of both their nature and their characteristics.
The current text merely distinguishes between two types, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and nature (*svabhāva*),
and does not separately establish them as "impurity of characteristics" and "impurity of nature.
One should instead combine the intermediate category and subsume it under nature.
Regarding ultimate impurity, as the verse in the treatise says:
"Examine this body with discernment; it will ultimately return to the place of death."
Their speech is difficult to address and they lack reciprocity;
they betray kindness like small children.
"Jù" (劇) means "extreme."
The "lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are as follows: the dung beetle (*śalabha*), also called the *kīṭaka* or *kīṭaka-śalabha*,
is precisely the insect that rolls dung into balls.
This worm knows only the taste of excrement,
yet cannot distinguish the flavor of the *modaka* (joy-pellets).
Next, the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkhānupaśyanā*) is explained.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, this body is entirely suffering;
every movement—bending, stretching, looking down, or looking up—is nothing but suffering.
Just as sitting is pleasant at first but becomes painful after a long time,
so it is with walking, standing, and lying down.
It is like the pursuit of female beauty when sexual desire is a source of pleasure.
The more one acquires it, the more severe the afflictions that arise;
it is like a case of scabies where the relief from fire becomes a cause of suffering.
Thus, the practitioner knows that the body is merely impermanent, suffering, and impure.
One must nurture them out of necessity.
It is like parents who give birth to a wicked son;
although the son is utterly evil, he was born from them.
One must certainly nurture and bring [the body] to fulfillment.
Yet, the body is actually devoid of pleasure. Why is this?
Because they lack self-mastery;
just as a person afflicted by wind cannot bend or stretch, walk or move about, or approach and withdraw,
and just as one with a diseased throat cannot speak.
For this reason, we know that the body is not autonomous;
thus it is said that amidst lower suffering, one perversely gives rise to the perception of pleasure.
According to various treatises, the three miserable realms should be taken as the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
This is called the supreme suffering:
when the five signs of decline appear to the devas,
great suffering arises at the moment their celestial pleasures perish.
That which is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*) [is found] among the gods; that which is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkha*) is found among humans.
Because it is constantly suffering from moment to moment, it is called "inferior."
Ordinary worldlings recklessly imagine this to be pleasure;
thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* says:
"It is like placing a single eyelash on the palm of the hand, yet not perceiving it."
If placed upon the eye, it causes injury and discomfort; likewise,
while ordinary beings are like the palm of a hand and do not perceive the eyelash of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*),
the wise are like the eye and give rise to extreme revulsion and fear toward its conditions.
Compared to the sufferings of the three miserable realms, these are merely minor sufferings.
However, the present text, following its underlying meaning, establishes the three types of suffering directly in relation to the human realm;
for even though they are minor sufferings, they nonetheless possess all three types of suffering.
One should not arbitrarily give rise to the perception of pleasure therein.
Thus, in the eleventh fascicle of the Mahāyāna Sūtra, Kāśyapa raises an objection:
"If one gives rise to the perception of pleasure regarding inferior suffering..."
Does one also give rise to the perception of pleasure regarding the suffering of lower rebirths, even down to the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging in the lower realms?
Those born in the lower realm are those of the three evil destinies;
those born in the middle realm are humans;
those born in the upper realm are devas.
Furthermore, one should also ask: "Does one produce the perception of suffering regarding inferior pleasure?
The Buddha said:
"It is as you have said; therefore, in the past, for the sake of Śreṇika, I spoke of the three types of suffering within the three types of sensation."
Since each and every feeling contains all three types of suffering,
the present text establishes the meaning of the three sufferings within the context of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Next, it clarifies this within the contemplation of impermanence (*anityatā-vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the phrase "like a bird tied up," as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"A bird enters a jar, and a net covers the mouth of the jar."
"The silk is torn and the bird flies away; the divine spirit follows along with karma.
The commentary states:
"One receives retribution by riding upon karma, just as a bird enters a jar."
Bound by karma as if veiled by fine gauze, when the fruit has expired,
one follows karma like a bird flying out through a hole in the gauze;
because one must necessarily pursue karma upon departing, it is called "following and running."
In this passage, the basket is used as a metaphor for the fruit and the jar as a metaphor for the cause.
The statement regarding "attaining the rope" follows the system of the Sarvāstivāda,
which establishes "the attainment of attainment" (prāptiprāpti).
Because the subsequently attained [cognition] gradually attains that which was previously attained,
it enables past karma to reach the future; thus,
within the Sarvāstivāda school, karma enters the past.
It extends into the future;
when the body dies and passes away, the retribution of the future arises.
Just as a single karma is established, one acquires that karmic dharma by means of a single great acquisition (*mahāprāpti*).
Furthermore, by means of the small acquisition (parigraha), one obtains the great acquisition;
in the second moment, by means of the three great acquisitions,
one obtains the two preceding acquisitions as well as the karma and its dharmas.
Because the acquisitions of the first moment are established simultaneously;
furthermore, the three minor acquisitions acquire the three preceding major ones,
such that nine dharmas are accomplished in the initial moment.
The twenty-seven factors of the third moment.
This meaning of "attainment" (prāpti) originates from the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Abhidharma).
The *Vyākhyāyukti* states: [text follows].
The first moment is established as the present;
the second moment is established as the past.
If there were no agent, [this would not occur].
The first moment is established as being in the present; the second moment is established as belonging to two time periods.
As for what is called the "agent," within the first moment there is only that which co-exists with the dharma.
In the second moment of thought, there is only the dharma that follows.
As for the term "simultaneous with the dharma" (dharmasahaja),
it refers to the primary dharma of the first moment, as well as its major and minor acquisitions (prāpti).
Regarding the statement "the dharma is subsequent":
because the second moment and those following it transform into dharmas based on each preceding moment,
the subsequent moments obtain the acquisitions (prāpti) of both the great and the small.
Regarding the statement that there is no agent:
even at the very first moment, there is merely the coexistence of dharmas;
this is also as explained regarding the first moment of "action."
In the second moment, there is both the simultaneous attainment of dharmas (*dharmasahabhu-prāpti*) and the subsequent attainment of dharmas (*dharma-pṛṣṭha-prāpti*).
Regarding the "subsequent attainment of dharmas," it is as explained previously in the discussion of the second moment within the process of action.
Regarding the phrase "arising together with the dharma," it refers to the simultaneous arising,
following the dharma, of one unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) and its respective major and minor acquisitions (*prāpti*).
Thus, in the second moment, there are three major acquisitions and three minor acquisitions.
Having obtained the first three dharmas,
there are simultaneously another three dharmas that arise together;
thus, in the second moment, nine dharmas arise together.
Together with the three factors of the first moment, these constitute twelve dharmas.
Thus, in the second moment, six acquisitions (prāpti) obtain the past [factors];
this is termed "accomplishment in the past."
Furthermore, there are two types of acquisition (*prāpti*) that acquire present dharmas,
which is termed "present accomplishment.
Therefore, it is said that at the first moment, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is accomplished in the present.
In the second moment of thought, non-manifestation (avijñapti) is accomplished across two time periods.
Generally speaking, when it is said that one "attains" the great or small [vows],
it is always by means of the great attainment (mahāprāpti) that one attains the fundamental dharma.
Furthermore, by means of a small attainment,
one attains a great attainment;
conversely, by means of a great attainment, one attains a small attainment.
Therefore, the large and the small can mutually attain one another.
Thus we know that the third mindfulness proceeds in this manner,
extending successively until it pervades all of space.
In all cases where one performs various karmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome, if the mind is inferior,
there is only the act (*kriyā*) and no non-act (*avijñapti*).
If the mind is superior, there is both the act and the non-act.
Both manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) each give rise to their own acquisitions (*prāpti*).
When karma enters the past, its acquisition extends even to the future,
capable of summoning subsequent retribution.
Since the unmanifest (avijñapti) is acquired only together with form,
it is therefore called "acquisition" (prāpti), which is neither matter nor mind.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that there are fourteen types of non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra).

This refers to categories such as acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*), the two meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti* and *nirodhasamāpatti*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the group of names (*nāmakāya*).
These are the acquisitions produced by a single volitional action (*karmacetanā*) within the course of one lifetime.

It is merely said that karma is formed through the conjunction of the mind with body and speech;
this is provisionally established as a "seed" that persists until future birth.
Furthermore, the designation "karma" applies generally to the preliminary, the fundamental, and the subsequent stages.

In the Mahāyāna, although there is this difference— that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) contains and sustains [seeds] until the next life—
the place where one receives retribution is nonetheless the same as that of ordinary beings.
It is inevitably ensnared by the four great elements of semen and blood;
until one has attained cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
it remains perpetually bound by the tether of acquisition (prāpti).
As long as the fetters have not been severed, one who has departed returns again.
When the present aggregates (skandhas) are destroyed, it is called "having departed";
when one undergoes rebirth once more, it is called "returning."
Only upon reaching the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-phala) is it called "breaking the cage.
When the karma for rebirth is exhausted, it is called "non-returning.
When the physical continuity of the aggregates (skandha) no longer persists, it is called "the empty cage remaining."
The phrase "this destruction, etc. further excludes ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
It refers to how, upon the destruction of these five aggregates (*skandha*), the aggregates of existence (*bhava-skandha*) arise;
it concerns the emergence from the aggregates and entry into the aggregates, such as birth in this life and the next, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the seal is destroyed and the inscription is formed," this further clarifies the metaphors of the basket and the jar, though the wording differs slightly.
These two metaphors of the basket and the jar serve merely to illustrate cause and effect.
This analogy of the wax seal further includes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra, fascicle twenty-seven, states:
"Just as when a wax seal is pressed into clay, the seal and the clay meet; as the seal disappears, the impression is formed."
The inscription does not emerge from the clay, nor does it come from any other place;
rather, it is formed through the causal conditions of the seal.
The Sūtra provides a corresponding analogy, stating:
When the aggregates of the present cease, the aggregates of the intermediate state arise.
These present aggregates do not transform into the five aggregates of the intermediate state;
nor do they arise from themselves, nor do they come from elsewhere.
Because the aggregates of the present life manifest, the aggregates of the intermediate state arise.
To provide an analogy for this conjunction:
it is like pressing a seal into clay; when the seal is removed, the impression is formed.
Although their names do not differ, their temporal periods are distinct.
Therefore, I say that the five aggregates of the intermediate state (antarābhava) are not seen by the fleshly eye, but are seen by the divine eye.

therefore, diligence takes the mind as its foundation and the body as its support.

Physical diligence is also like this. Furthermore,
diligence is like a wild pheasant seeing a great forest being consumed by fire.

he used his own physical strength to fly into the water,
soaking his feathers and returning to extinguish the great fire.

At that time, the Lord of Devas came and asked him:

Question: To what extent will this exertion of yours continue?

"I shall take death as my deadline.

"If this is not false, may the fire be extinguished at once.
